articles.body: Carbon Capture Usage & Storage October 23, 2026 · 1 minute ago Petronas, TotalEnergies and Mitsui to develop CO2 storage area off Peninsular Malaysia NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Development of Southern CCS Hub. Source: Petronas PETRONAS CCS Ventures (PCCSV), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Malaysia’s state-owned oil & gas firm Petronas, TotalEnergies EP CCS Malaysia and Mitsui & Co. have entered into a joint venture agreement (JVA) to develop a CO2 storage area offshore Peninsular Malaysia. The partners previously signed a carbon capture and storage (CCS) agreement in 2023 , as part of which they performed development studies and technical evaluations of potential storage areas offshore Peninsular Malaysia. In 2025, the partnership progressed into a key principles agreement, which laid the groundwork for front-end engineering and design (FEED) activities and the formation of the joint venture structure. With the JVA in place, the framework is set for incorporating a dedicated joint venture company to progress the development, commercialization, and operation of the carbon storage area offshore Peninsular Malaysia, described as a key component of Malaysia's Southern CCS Hub. The Southern CCS Hub is being developed to receive CO2 domestically and regionally, including potential cross-border CO2 shipments. The first phase primarily targets a depleted gas field with an expected injection capacity of up to 5 million tons per annum (mtpa), with first injection targeted as early as 2031, in line with industry readiness. Petronas, TotalEnergies and Mitsui will now focus on advancing the technical and commercial maturity of the initial carbon storage project ahead of a final investment decision (FID). "The Joint Venture Agreement is a reflection of the strong partnership we have built with our strategic partners over the years. From our early development studies through to FEED activities, we have worked closely together to mature this opportunity and establish a shared vision for the Southern CCS Hub," said Emry Hisham Yusoff , PCCSV’s Chief Executive Officer. "By bringing together PETRONAS’ subsurface expertise, with their global CCS experience, commercial and logistics capabilities, we are confident in maintaining this momentum towards achieving Final Investment Decision (FID) in the near future while advancing Malaysia’s ambition to become a leading regional CCS hub.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: IFM-managed fund agrees to acquire majority stake in Associated British Ports
articles.summary: A fund managed by IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a 63.9% stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), one of the United Kingdom’s largest port operators. articles.body: A fund managed by IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a 63.9% stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), one of the United Kingdom’s largest port operators. The agreement involves the acquisition of the entire shareholdings held by Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and OMERS. CPP Investments will sell its 33.9% interest, while OMERS will divest its 30% stake. The transaction will give the IFM-managed fund majority ownership of ABP, subject to the required approvals. The financial terms of the agreement have not been disclosed. Completion is expected during the first half of 2027. Major investment in UK port infrastructure Associated British Ports plays a significant role in the UK’s maritime and logistics sectors. Its network handles approximately a quarter of the country’s seaborne trade. The company operates major port facilities, including Southampton, Immingham and Hull. These ports support container shipping, automotive logistics, bulk cargo and other commercial activities. The proposed acquisition represents a significant ownership change for a major UK port infrastructure business. It also highlights the continued involvement of institutional investors in maritime infrastructure. Transaction expected to close in 2027 The agreement will see CPP Investments and OMERS exit their existing investments in ABP. The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including the necessary regulatory approvals. Until these requirements are satisfied, the existing ownership arrangements remain in place. The companies expect the transaction to be completed in the first half of 2027. The announcement confirms the agreed transfer of the majority stake but does not disclose the purchase price. Following completion, the IFM-managed fund will hold a controlling interest in one of the UK’s most important port infrastructure operators.

articles.title: OEG books three more offshore wind CTVs at Diverse Marine
articles.summary: UK offshore services player OEG Marine Services has ordered three crew transfer vessels (CTVs) from Isle of Wight shipbuilder Diverse Marine as part of its offshore wind fleet expansion and renewal programme. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables OEG books three more offshore wind CTVs at Diverse Marine Bojan Lepic October 23, 2026 0 0 1 minute read OEG OEG UK offshore services player OEG Marine Services has ordered three crew transfer vessels (CTVs) from Isle of Wight shipbuilder Diverse Marine as part of its offshore wind fleet expansion and renewal programme. The vessels, based on Chartwell Marine’s Brevity SL class design, are scheduled for delivery throughout 2027. Each vessel will measure 26 m in length, with a load line length of less than 24 m, and will be built at Diverse Marine’s Cowes facility. The first vessel will feature quad Volvo Penta IPS propulsion compliant with IMO Tier III emissions standards, alongside Hull Vane transom foils designed to improve fuel efficiency at cruising speeds. All three newbuilds will share the same specification, be classed by Bureau Veritas and operate under the UK flag. The vessels are expected to support construction activities at an offshore wind project off the UK’s east coast in 2027, working alongside OEG’s existing Chartwell-designed Fulmar and Furioso . The order marks the second collaboration between OEG and Diverse Marine following the delivery of the Fulmar in 2025. That vessel has since supported construction work at Scotland’s Inch Cape offshore wind farm. OEG director Leif Cooper said the Chartwell design performed better than expected, prompting the company to return to Diverse Marine for additional vessels. articles.title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
articles.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 38 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.body: Essar Ports has received a Letter of Award (LoA) from India’s Deendayal Port Authority to develop a new multipurpose cargo terminal at Tuna Tekra, Kandla. The project represents an investment of approximately INR 22.76 billion. Once completed, the terminal will have an annual cargo-handling capacity of 18.33 million tonnes. The development will take place under a public-private partnership (PPP) model, with Essar Ports and the port authority contributing to the investment. New terminal to increase cargo capacity The planned terminal will feature four berths with a combined length of 1,200 metres. It will be able to accommodate vessels of up to 170,000 deadweight tonnes (DWT). Essar Ports is expected to invest approximately INR 15.53 billion in the project. The Deendayal Port Authority will contribute around INR 7.23 billion. The terminal will be developed under a Build–Operate–Transfer (BOT) model. The concession agreement will cover a period of 30 years. The new facilities will expand cargo-handling capacity at Kandla, one of India’s major ports on the country’s western coast. The project will also support the port’s ability to handle larger vessels and a wider range of cargo operations. Essar strengthens its port infrastructure portfolio The award marks another step in Essar Ports’ expansion of its maritime infrastructure activities. The planned terminal will add new capacity for multipurpose cargo handling. It will also strengthen the port infrastructure available to businesses moving goods through the region. The investment forms part of efforts to improve port facilities and support maritime trade in India. However, the Letter of Award represents a project development milestone rather than the start of commercial operations. The announcement does not provide a confirmed construction timetable or opening date for the new terminal.

articles.title: Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset
articles.summary: PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE.
articles.body: Business & Finance October 23, 2026 · 1 hour ago Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Hail and Ghasha island under construction Source ADNOC As one of the world’s largest sour gas mega-projects continues to take shape in the waters of the Arabian Gulf, two energy heavyweights, Thailand’s PTT Exploration and Production Public Company (PTTEP) and Italy’s Eni, have pooled their stakes in Abu Dhabi’s massive Ghasha concession, carving out a newly minted joint venture (JV) called Seela Energies to unlock financing, share deep technical expertise, and scale up their activities for the long haul. PTTEP MENA, PTTEP’s wholly owned subsidiary, together with Eni Abu Dhabi, has established Seela Energies, with each company holding a 50% shareholding. Each of the founders holds a 10% participating interest in the Ghasha concession project , which will now be transferred to the newly formed JV. As a result, the duo will hold an indirect 10% interest in the project. According to PTTEP, all required regulatory, governmental, and partner approvals have been obtained, and all conditions precedent have been fulfilled. “The establishment of Seela Energies strengthens the collaboration between PTTEP and Eni, enhances access to financing, builds capability, shares expertise and supports potential future mutual growth in Middle East region, in line with PTTEP’s strategy to deliver long-term value through strategic partnerships,” emphasized the Thai player. Related Articles Fossil Energy WATCH: First steel cut for mega gas project set on zero-emission ops by entwining smart tech, carbon capture, hydrogen, nuclear, and renewable power 7 min read The Ghasha concession offshore Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, which is operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), is expected to produce more than 1.8 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 150,000 barrels of oil and condensate per day over the long term. This concession is considered to be one of the world's largest sulfur-rich gas development projects and a cornerstone of the UAE's strategy to achieve gas self-sufficiency and support rising international export demand. The development concept encompasses multiple fields, including Hail and Ghasha , located in shallow waters. This project utilizes a series of artificial islands rather than traditional platforms to drill and manage operations while minimizing environmental disturbance. Related Articles Fossil Energy First jacket comes to slide into place at huge offshore gas project 3 min read The Hail and Ghasha project, designed with an emphasis on low-emissions technology, aims to operate with net-zero carbon emissions by integrating carbon capture with a target of around 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year, low-carbon hydrogen use to replace fuel gas, and relying on less-emission-intensive power sources, such as nuclear and solar. ADNOC’s partners in the Ghasha concession, aside from Eni and PTTEP, which consolidated their joint stakes under Seela Energies, involved other companies across the broader project lifecycle, including Wintershall Dea, OMV, and Lukoil. The Ghasha development is envisioned to employ smart technology across all operations, allowing operators, technicians, and site personnel remote access to the project’s operations. Aside from a fully unmanned facility, ADNOC has set its sights on artificial intelligence (AI), such as predictive maintenance, for all critical rotating equipment. A few months ago, the operator, in partnership with Eni and PTTEP, put into place a structured financing transaction of up to $11 billion (AED 40.4 billion) for Hail and Ghasha sour gas development. The UAE giant’s financing model follows a series of midstream and infrastructure transactions, including a $4.9 billion (AED 18 billion) oil pipeline partnership and a $10.1 billion (AED 37.1 billion) gas pipeline agreement. It also comes after build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) projects, such as the $3.8 billion (AED 14 billion) project to power and decarbonize offshore operations and the $2.2 billion (AED 8.3 billion) project to deliver sustainable water supplies to onshore operations. articles.body: Tanker Oil Spill Forces Closure of Beaches in UAE Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Алексей Закиров / Adobe Stock An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, prompting containment operations and environmental assessments, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. The ministry said all beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain had been temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. The announcement followed reports of a strange odour by residents in some emirates on social media. The ministry said that odours reported by residents in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain posed no health risks to them. The ministry did not say what caused the spill, and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. The spill adds to heightened concern over maritime security in Gulf waters after a series of attacks on commercial vessels, including incidents outside the Strait of Hormuz. On October 9, a vessel, identified by shipping sources as GEM No.2, was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE, causing a fire that was later extinguished. While no group claimed responsibility, maritime security sources told Reuters the incident occurred outside the Strait of Hormuz and pointed to a widening of risks for commercial shipping. Earlier that week, a tanker was also struck off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf. The spill also follows a separate tanker-related environmental incident in the region. In August, oil from a tanker that ran aground off Oman began reaching the mainland coast, prompting concerns about environmental damage and cleanup efforts. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 202 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. Register On 28 September, APM Capital agreed to acquire a 53.35% stake in the parent of Euroports, an operator of more than 50 deep-sea and inland terminals across ten European countries and China that handles over 70 million tonnes of bulk, breakbulk and liquid bulk a year. On 20 October in Copenhagen, APM Terminals signed a memorandum of understanding with Vietnamese conglomerate Hateco for a rail freight terminal network in northern Vietnam valued at up to US$3.5 billion. They are two parallel tracks of a single strategy. APM Terminals, Maersk’s port unit, runs container terminals, and its investments follow the corridors that geopolitics is redrawing. Vietnam shows the template. APM began as an adviser to Hateco in 2023, took a 49% stake in the Haiphong international container terminal in April 2026, joined the Lien Chieu port project in Danang, and is now moving to the railhead. Each step pushes control further from the quay into the hinterland. The same logic runs through on-dock rail at Mobile, the rail-heavy Rijeka Gateway in Croatia, and Balboa in Panama, where APM took over operations in February after Panama’s Supreme Court annulled CK Hutchison’s concessions. APM Capital is a separate infrastructure fund manager backed by A.P. Moller Holding, and it invests where the container business does not reach. Euroports moves fertilizers, grain, sugar, metals and forest products, the commodities that keep European industry and food systems running. Coming after APMC’s investment in Spain’s BERGÉ Logistics, the deal gives the group a layered presence in Iberia: APM Terminals’ container gateways at Valencia and Barcelona, with bulk, breakbulk and logistics around them. APMC chief executive Kim Fejfer framed the purchase in the language of resilient supply chains and secure trade flows. Belgium’s public investors SFPIM and PMV remain Euroports shareholders, with SFPIM saying it intends to keep strategic assets anchored in Belgium. The Hateco agreement was signed during the state visit of Vietnam’s General Secretary and President Tô Lâm to Denmark. Balboa was handed over after the Panama Maritime Authority took possession of the port by decree. In each case the Maersk position is co-owned or endorsed by the government that hosts it. That is the reverse of the exposure that cost CK Hutchison its Panama ports. Panama Ports Company has brought arbitration in London against Maersk over Balboa, proceedings likely to take years. Euroports still needs regulatory approvals, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and its footprint includes terminals in China: a group building alternatives to Chinese port networks will hold assets under Chinese jurisdiction. Headline figures also run ahead of committed money. Hateco valued its earlier Haiphong port project with Maersk at US$400 million, roughly a ninth of the new rail ceiling, and Vietnam’s double-digit growth target is itself exposed to fuel disruption from the Iran war. Operating risk sits with APM Terminals, balance-sheet flexibility with A.P. Moller Capital, and political legitimacy is borrowed from host states. Where CMA CGM orchestrates its network with as few hard assets as possible, the APM Group layers them, across cargo types and transport modes, on corridors aligned with the West. Three markers will show whether the model holds: Panama’s long-term tender for Balboa, regulatory clearance for Euroports, and the first binding commitment under the Vietnam memorandum.
takeaways: One arm operates container terminals on contested corridors, the other buys the bulk ports that feed European industry.
Together they form a single strategy of corridor control.
Within three weeks, two deals carrying the Maersk family name redrew the map of its port ambitions.

The company has established operations in Freetown, Shanghai and Geneva. articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 108 1 minute read Icon Energy Icon Energy Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions. Its most recent disclosed commercial moves include fixing the 63,668 dwt ultramax Charlie on an index-linked charter extending into 2027 and acquiring a minority investment in two containership projects. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Corpus Christi LNG terminal operated by Cheniere Energy on the La Quinta Ship Channel in Corpus Christi, Texas, USA. Source: Bechtel In a move that reflects long-term energy planning, the U.S. Gulf Coast is locking in its commercial ties for the next three decades, as U.S.-headquartered energy player Cheniere has shown with a landmark liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal with Qatar’s state-owned oil and gas giant QatarEnergy, signing on to deliver millions of tonnes of LNG straight through 2054. Cheniere Energy’s subsidiaries, Sabine Pass Liquefaction (SPL) and Corpus Christi Liquefaction (CCL) , have each entered into long-term LNG sale and purchase agreements (SPAs) with QatarEnergy to supply a total of 4 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of LNG through 2054. Jack Fusco , Cheniere’s Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer, commented: “These pivotal, multi-decade agreements with QatarEnergy, one of the world’s most important energy companies and a cornerstone of the global LNG industry, represent a major long-term commercial commitment and reinforce Cheniere’s position as the leader in U.S. LNG. “We take pride that Cheniere’s track record of operational excellence, reliability and long-term customer focus provided the foundation for this landmark commercial relationship with QatarEnergy. We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century.” While confirming the two SPAs for the purchase of LNG from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi facilities in Louisiana and Texas respectively, located along the United States Gulf Coast, QatarEnergy explained that these deals reflect its continued confidence in the long-term role of LNG in the global energy mix and its efforts to further develop a flexible, diversified, and globally competitive LNG portfolio. The SPAs were signed by Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi , Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs, President and CEO of QatarEnergy, and Jack Fusco , Chairman, President and CEO of Cheniere Energy. Minister Al-Kaabi said: “The signing of these two SPAs marks an important milestone in our LNG strategy. This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market. “The additional volumes will complement QatarEnergy’s existing LNG supplies, enhance our supply and trading portfolio, and strengthen our ability to serve customers across the globe.” The Qatari giant has agreed to purchase 2 mtpa of LNG from each of SPL and CCL on a free-on-board (FOB) basis for a purchase price indexed to the Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. The deliveries under the SPAs will begin in the early 2030s and continue through the end of 2054, with 1 mtpa of the SPL SPA subject to a positive final investment decision (FID) for the first phase of the SPL Expansion project. This phase has an expected total production capacity of over 6 mtpa of LNG, inclusive of estimated debottlenecking opportunities. In May 2026, the lump sum, turnkey engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract was penned with Bechtel Energy for the first phase of the SPL Expansion project, and the firm was given the go-ahead for early engineering and procurement under a limited notice to proceed (LNTP). articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Greater China Taylor Maritime agrees final owned bulker sale ahead of London exit Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 153 1 minute read London-listed Taylor Maritime has agreed to sell its last owned bulk carrier for $15.1m, taking its fleet disposal programme to 56 vessels and putting total proceeds on course to reach almost $933m. The Ed Buttery-led company said the final sale is expected to complete in December, bringing to an end a three-year selling campaign that has steadily dismantled one of the largest geared dry bulk fleets in the market. Since the beginning of 2023, Taylor Maritime has executed 55 vessel disposals with expected gross proceeds of $917.7m, at an average discount of 3.5% to fair market value. The latest agreement will lift the total to approximately $932.8m once completed. The move follows the completion of three handysize disposals announced earlier this month, which generated $48.6m. Those deals included transactions involving Buttery’s privately controlled T3 Holding vehicle, which acquired one vessel outright and a majority stake in a company holding another two handysizes alongside Hermes World Maritime. While the latest agreement covers Taylor Maritime’s last owned ship, one vessel remains on charter under a sale-and-leaseback arrangement with a purchase option. That contract expires in April 2027, and the company is assessing the most efficient way to exit the arrangement. Taylor Maritime expects to cease all commercial shipping operations by the end of 2026, with the wind-down now moving towards its final shareholder distributions. The company has confirmed a fourth compulsory capital return of $45m in November, taking the amount returned to investors since January to $263.4m. A further redemption is expected to be announced in December, subject to completion of the remaining vessel sale. The board then intends to put forward plans to cancel the company’s London listing. Taylor Maritime, which floated in May 2021, built its fleet to more than 50 vessels following the takeover of Grindrod Shipping before reversing course and embarking on an extensive asset disposal programme. The company formally adopted a managed realisation strategy in March this year, prioritising vessel sales and the return of capital to shareholders over continued fleet operations. The official launch at the Hydrogen and Carbon Capture Technology World Expo was attended by Hamburg’s Senator for...
articles.body: eFUEL GROUP and DACMA GmbH have opened the DACMA Competence Center at Hamburg Blue Hub, combining the testing of modular CO2 capture technologies with preparations for international applications. The official launch at the Hydrogen and Carbon Capture Technology World Expo was attended by Hamburg’s Senator for Economic Affairs Dr Melanie Leonhard and Evelyne Coulombe of the Canadian Embassy, whose participation underlined the significance of German-Canadian cooperation in direct air capture technology. The Competence Center tests modular DAC plants under real industrial conditions, examining technical components and materials, analysing operating processes and energy and material flows, and developing approaches for technical optimisation in collaboration with international universities and research institutions. Direct Air Capture refers to the capture of CO2 from ambient air, which can be used as a carbon source for synthetic fuels and other chemical products, or stored permanently underground to achieve net atmospheric CO2 removal. A central element of the centre’s work is the partnership between DACMA and Canadian project developer Deep Sky, which includes a first DACMA plant with a planned capture capacity of 600 tonnes of CO2 per year and the joint development of next-generation technology for larger plants. Deep Sky combines atmospheric CO2 capture with permanent geological storage, with a long-term target of removing one million tonnes of CO2 from the atmosphere annually at scale. Senator Leonhard described the Competence Center as creating new opportunities for companies and researchers to test how CO2 from ambient air can be used as a raw material for industry, including the development of synthetic fuels needed in aviation and shipping, strengthening Hamburg as a centre of innovation. Alex Petre, CEO of Deep Sky, described real-world deployment as the decisive step in understanding technology performance and scaling carbon removal to industrial levels. Alexander Backs, Co-CEO of DACMA, emphasised the value of feeding continuous operational experience directly back into development. Lorenz Kiene, Managing Director of eFUEL GROUP, highlighted the focus on integrating DAC into eFuels, eSAF and eMethanol production chains as a key objective for the centre.

articles.title: New index tracks how much the world cares about shipping
articles.summary: A new online index – much trailed on Splash – measuring how much attention the global shipping industry receives has gone live, offering maritime companies a way to assess public interest in shipping news and major incidents. Created by crisis communications specialist Dustin Eno, the Maritime Attention Index...
articles.body: Operations New index tracks how much the world cares about shipping Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 287 1 minute read Maxar Technologies Maxar Technologies A new online index – much trailed on Splash – measuring how much attention the global shipping industry receives has gone live, offering maritime companies a way to assess public interest in shipping news and major incidents. Created by crisis communications specialist Dustin Eno, the Maritime Attention Index combines Google searches, Wikipedia page views, social media activity and mainstream news coverage into a single daily score. “I built the index to answer a simple question with a single number: how much attention is shipping getting right now?” Eno explained. “Media monitoring tells you how much is being published about shipping, not how much attention it gets.” The publicly accessible platform allows users to examine historical attention spikes, compare incidents and identify how quickly public interest fades. Disasters such as the Ever Given, Wakashio and Dali casualties all show spikes. Eno’s analysis also reveals remarkably consistent patterns in how interest fades after major maritime incidents. When adjusted for duration and intensity, the attention curve surrounding this year’s Iran conflict closely resembles those generated by the Ever Given grounding and Baltimore bridge collapse. The index, which Eno has previously used in Splash commentary, is now available as an interactive public resource, accompanied by monthly analysis. Today’s reading stands at 69.3, with a score of 50 deemed normal. By way of comparison, in the opening fortnight of the US attacks on Iran in March this year, the index shot up to 332.3 points. The index goes back to the start of the 2020s, with its all-time high being the Ever Given’s closure of the Suez Canal in 2021. articles.title: Port of Los Angeles Reports Record Low Emissions
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles recorded its lowest emissions per container on record in 2025, continuing a two-decade decline in air pollution even as container throughput remained near historic highs.According to the port's newly released Inventory of Air Emissions…
articles.body: Port of Los Angeles Reports Record Low Emissions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 Image courtesy Port of Los Angeles The Port of Los Angeles recorded its lowest emissions per container on record in 2025, continuing a two-decade decline in air pollution even as container throughput remained near historic highs. According to the port's newly released Inventory of Air Emissions, diesel particulate matter (DPM) emissions declined 2% in 2025 compared with 2024, while nitrogen oxides (NOx) fell 4%, sulfur oxides (SOx) decreased 5% and greenhouse gas emissions dropped 3%. The NOx reduction brought annual emissions to their lowest level since the port began tracking air pollution in 2005. The improvements came as Los Angeles handled nearly 10.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), maintaining its position as the nation's busiest container port. Since 2005, the port has reduced DPM emissions by 90%, NOx by 72%, SOx by 98% and greenhouse gases by 16%, while container volumes increased 37%. Much of the progress reflects investments in cleaner vessels, cargo-handling equipment and landside transportation. Ocean-going vessels have reduced DPM emissions by 94% and SOx by 98% since 2005, aided by cleaner fuels, shore power and emissions capture technologies. Harbor craft are also contributing. In 2025, 55% of tugs, barges, ferries and other workboats met Tier 3 or Tier 4 emissions standards, compared with 20% in 2017. Harbor craft DPM emissions have fallen 69% since 2005. Electric cargo-handling equipment increased 20% during 2025, with zero-emission units now representing 14% of the port's equipment fleet. Meanwhile, truck-related DPM and NOx emissions declined 16% and 25%, respectively, year over year. "These results demonstrate that we can move high cargo volumes while continuing to reduce emissions," said Port Executive Director Gene Seroka. The findings reflect ongoing implementation of the San Pedro Bay ports' Clean Air Action Plan, including investments in zero-emission equipment, charging infrastructure and cleaner maritime operations.

articles.title: New Crewsure Energy Program Provides Employee Benefits for Offshore Workers
articles.summary: Crewsure Insurance Services Limited (Crewsure) has announced the launch of Crewsure Energy, a new program that brings together traditional employee benefits with specialist Crisis Response protection, designed for companies employing personnel…
articles.body: New Crewsure Energy Program Provides Employee Benefits for Offshore Workers Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Crewsure Insurance Services Limited Crewsure Insurance Services Limited (Crewsure) has announced the launch of Crewsure Energy, a new program that brings together traditional employee benefits with specialist Crisis Response protection, designed for companies employing personnel working in the international energy and offshore sectors. The launch represents an expansion for Crewsure, as the company already provides specialist MLC crew benefits for personnel working aboard drilling ships and other maritime assets. Crewsure Energy now extends that expertise beyond the vessel to provide dedicated protection for employees and contractors working on offshore rigs and other declared energy operations. At its core are emergency medical expenses, personal accident and wages protection, with worldwide cover available subject to the policy terms and schedule. The medical section covers medical emergency treatment following illness or accident, while personal accident protection includes accidental death and permanent disability benefits and loss of wages cover and loss of baggage. The program also recognizes the operational consequences for an employer when a member of an overseas workforce can no longer continue their assignment. Cover can therefore include reasonable additional costs of recruiting and sending a replacement employee overseas following death, illness, bodily injury or qualifying compulsory quarantine. A distinguishing feature of Crewsure Energy is its integrated Crisis Response protection. Rather than treating employee benefits and security risks entirely separately, the program can respond to events including kidnap, detention, disappearance, hijack, hostage crisis, extortion, threats and virtual kidnap, with access to professional response consultants. Crisis benefits can extend considerably beyond the immediate incident, including response consultant costs, travel and accommodation, loss of salary, replacement key-person costs, legal and medical expenses, rehabilitation and job retraining, temporary security measures and other specified additional expenses. The program can also provide Emergency Political Repatriation and Relocation and Threat Repatriation, including specified travel and accommodation costs and, in qualifying circumstances, personal effects left behind and irrevocably lost following an emergency political repatriation. Emergency medical, inpatient and evacuation/repatriation assistance is supported by Northcott Global Solutions, with 24-hour assistance available, while the Crisis Response section provides access to specialist response consultants. The Medical Insurance, Personal Accident Insurance, Sick Pay and Crisis Response insurance is underwritten by certain underwriters at Lloyd's of London.

articles.title: Shipbuilding: Bayonne Drydock Gets MARAD Grant
articles.summary: Bayonne Drydock & Repair Corp. has secured a $673,123 grant from the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD) to upgrade surface preparation equipment and expand workforce training at its ship repair facility in the Port of New York and New Jersey.Awarded through MARAD's Small Shipyard Grant Program…
articles.body: Shipbuilding: Bayonne Drydock Gets MARAD Grant Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 Members of Bayonne Drydock’s Executive Leadership Team pose with Congressman Rob Menendez, NJ State Senator Angela McKnight, NJ Assemblyman Jerry Walker, Mayor Sharon Nadrowski, and Bayonne City Council Image courtesy BDD Bayonne Drydock & Repair Corp. has secured a $673,123 grant from the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD) to upgrade surface preparation equipment and expand workforce training at its ship repair facility in the Port of New York and New Jersey. Awarded through MARAD's Small Shipyard Grant Program , the funding will be combined with the shipyard's own investment to purchase automated ultra-high-pressure hydro-blasting and surface preparation equipment. The improvements are intended to increase productivity, reduce vessel turnaround times and enhance the yard's ability to service commercial and government vessels. The investment includes an integrated robotic hydro-blasting system, an additional surface preparation unit and supporting spare parts. Funding will also support training for the shipyard's workforce of more than 300 employees, enabling personnel to operate and maintain the new equipment. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize our surface-preparation infrastructure with state-of-the-art robotic technology," said Ryan Patrick Woerner, Executive Vice President and General Counsel of Bayonne Drydock. Woerner said the additional equipment will improve operational productivity, limit downtime and provide employees with tools to support maritime readiness. The latest award continues a series of MARAD-supported capital improvements at the Bayonne facility. In 2018, the shipyard received $1.08 million for upgrades to its graving dock and welding equipment. Another $730,477 grant followed in 2023 for hydro-blasting equipment and telehandlers. Founded in 1997, Bayonne Drydock operates a full-service repair facility at the former Military Ocean Terminal in Bayonne, New Jersey. Its principal infrastructure includes a 1,092-foot graving dock and a 1,280-metric-ton mobile boat hauler. The yard provides scheduled maintenance, drydocking, heavy repairs and emergency services for commercial and government vessels. articles.title: Empire State VII to Return to New York After Months-Long Navy Mission Plans Scrapped
articles.summary: SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy SUNY Maritime College SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment supporting the U.S. Navy. The reversal comes just weeks after the vessel departed New York for Norfolk, Virginia, where it was scheduled to undergo maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of a classified national security mission. In an October 21 message to the college community, SUNY Maritime President Rear Admiral John A. Okon confirmed the change. “I am pleased to share an important update on Empire State VII. The federal activation plan has changed, and the ship is now expected to return to Fort Schuyler for academic use, ship work, and with watches resuming no later than the middle of November,” Okon wrote. The announcement marks a significant shift from the original plans outlined by the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), which ordered the vessel’s activation in August for an anticipated 170-day federal mission. An August 28 decision memorandum reviewed by gCaptain said the ship was needed to meet an urgent Military Sealift Command requirement and that no other suitable vessel was available within the required timeframe. Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel described the activation as a “compelling strategic necessity.” The ship subsequently departed New York for Norfolk on September 30, with plans to remain there through October 30 for maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of follow-on operations supporting the Navy. The nature and destination of those operations were never publicly disclosed. It remains unclear what prompted the change in plans, whether the original military requirement has been withdrawn or reassigned, or how much of the planned work in Norfolk has been completed. For SUNY Maritime, however, the early return is welcome news. The vessel’s absence had threatened to disrupt academic programs, shipboard training and the sea time cadets need to qualify for U.S. Coast Guard licenses. “Empire State is more than a training ship. It is a classroom, a laboratory, and an essential part of the Maritime experience,” Okon said. Okon previously warned that losing the ship for much of the academic year would create significant challenges, and he pressed MARAD to return the vessel by February to keep the college’s 2027 Summer Sea Term on schedule. The revised timeline would bring the ship home roughly three months earlier than that requested deadline. Empire State VII , delivered in 2023, is the first of five purpose-built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) developed by MARAD. The ships are designed primarily to train future merchant marine officers while also providing the federal government with additional sealift and emergency response capabilities. The vessel’s activation was expected to provide an early test of the NSMV program’s dual-use concept, demonstrating how a federally owned training ship could be called into service for national security missions. Instead, the shortened deployment raises questions about the circumstances behind the original urgent military requirement and the subsequent decision to release the vessel. “We will continue working with MARAD to confirm the exact details of the ship’s return and ensure we are ready to resume normal operations,” Okon said. articles.summary: Oil prices climbed about 2% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region.Brent futures rose $2.42, or 2.2%, to $111.24 a barrel at 10:45 a.m.
articles.body: Houthi Attacks Drive Oil Prices to Five-Month High Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Adobe Stock/vadish Oil prices climbed about 2% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region. Brent futures rose $2.42, or 2.2%, to $111.24 a barrel at 10:45 a.m. EDT (1445 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose $1.14, or 1.2%, to $98.29. That drove Brent into technically overbought territory for a third time in a week and set for its highest close since May 18. Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Houthis intensifies. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned group pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth. "Reports of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and on its oil infrastructure," PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said. "No de-escalation is anticipated until the US midterm elections, which should keep oil prices elevated." Morgan Stanley analysts estimated that Middle East crude oil exports were around 17 million barrels per day last week. Crude exports from the region averaged about 18 million bpd in the 12 months before the start of the Iran war, according to Kpler. In the US, refiner Valero Energy posted its highest-ever quarterly profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict sent refining margins soaring during the third quarter. AROUND THE WORLD Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the two sides kept up a barrage despite the latest US push to end the war. Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November. Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices. Any deal to end the war which began with Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 could allow Russia to export more. Senior Russian political and energy officials urged the European Union on Thursday to reconsider its plans to ban imports of Russian LNG, arguing the bloc's low storage levels had put Europe in a precarious position. The European Parliament, meanwhile, approved a three-year delay to EU methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports, after pressure from governments including France and the US. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. (Reuters)

articles.body: Citi: Oil Prices Remain Unstable Despite Recovering Gulf Exports Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Photo courtesy OOCL China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new analysis from BIMCO. The global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2 million compensated gross tonnage (CGT) as of September 1, 2026, up 13% from 180 million CGT a year earlier. While slightly below the all-time high of 210.4 million CGT reached in May, the backlog remains above the previous record of 195.4 million CGT set in 2008. Chinese shipyards have been the biggest beneficiaries of the ordering boom, securing 74% of all CGT contracted over the past 12 months. China now controls 64% of the global order book, well ahead of South Korea at 19% and Japan at just 6%. China’s lead is even more pronounced across the major commercial shipping sectors. Its yards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main vessel categories, including containerships, tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, other dry cargo ships and RoRo vessels. Together, those segments account for 88% of the global order book. Containerships are driving much of the growth. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” said Niels Rasmussen, BIMCO’s Chief Shipping Analyst. Chinese yards hold an especially commanding 81% share of the global containership order book. But the massive backlog also presents a growing challenge for shipbuilders, particularly in China, where scheduled deliveries are set to far exceed recent production levels. Based on each country’s highest annual output between 2021 and 2025, Chinese shipyards have enough orders to keep them busy for an average of 4.2 years. That compares with just 1.9 years for South Korean yards and 1.7 years for Japanese yards. The challenge is the sheer volume of ships scheduled for delivery. Combined output from China, South Korea and Japan reached 40.1 million CGT in 2025, but scheduled deliveries climb to 55.9 million CGT in 2027 and 60 million CGT in 2028. China faces the steepest increase, with its shipyards scheduled to deliver a record 44 million CGT in 2028, nearly double the 22.7 million CGT delivered in 2025. Meeting those commitments will require a significant increase in production capacity. BIMCO estimates that if capacity is instead measured against the highest annual output delivered or scheduled between 2021 and 2030, China’s order book coverage falls to 2.1 years, compared with 1.6 years for both South Korea and Japan. The figures highlight a potential downside to China’s rapid shipbuilding expansion. While its yards currently enjoy an enormous backlog, the investments needed to meet delivery commitments could leave the industry with excess capacity if demand for new ships slows. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver,” Rasmussen said. “The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. articles.title: Putin’s War On Ukraine Puts Oil Giant Rosneft Under Mounting Pressure
articles.summary: Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life.

(Source: Rosneft) (Bloomberg) — Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life. Hundreds of miles of pipeline now connected oil fields to storage tanks and a new port for Vostok Oil, part of an almost $50 billion investment. With Putin watching by video link, Sechin, the powerful head of state-run Rosneft PJSC, asked to begin loading the first tanker with crude. “Permission granted,” Putin said. The ceremony carried particular weight for Russia’s increasingly battered oil industry. Years of war and sanctions are making it harder for oil producers — including Rosneft, the nation’s largest — to maintain volumes today while developing reserves for tomorrow. Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project was supposed to show Russia could still do both. Sechin said it would add as much as 10% to the country’s current output by 2030 and supply millions of barrels to world markets for a century or more. But the milestone obscured a more complicated reality: Years behind schedule, Vostok Oil is still far from becoming Russia’s new oil province. The vast majority of crude flowing through the costly new Arctic network has been diverted from fields that have been producing for years. Just before the terminal opened in September, new oilfields in the Payakha cluster, expected to become key assets of Vostok Oil, accounted for less than 5% of its flows, according to a person familiar with the data, who asked not to be identified to discuss sensitive matters that aren’t public. Satellite imagery shows development continuing, but bringing those fields up to scale will require years more work and investment, according to Bloomberg analysis of the imagery and conversations with analysts. “The development of the company’s fields is carried out in a planned manner, which allows maximum efficiency to be extracted both from existing fields and from new projects,” Rosneft said in a statement, adding that production ramp-ups at Vostok Oil depend on market needs and general economic conditions. Viktor Kurilov, a senior analyst on the oil markets team at Rystad Energy, said building out Vostok Oil “is just one of the challenges Rosneft — and the Russian oil industry — is facing.” Among them is Ukraine’s dramatically expanded campaign of drone strikes against the country’s oil sector, which is inching closer to Vostok Oil facilities and repeatedly damaging refineries run by Rosneft and others in the European part of Russia. One of its biggest, Ryazan, which supplies fuel to Moscow and surrounding regions, has been shut for more than half the time since it was first attacked in May and has run well below full capacity when operating, according to damage assessments seen by Bloomberg. In turn, Rosneft’s finances are suffering. The company’s profits are falling and debt is rising despite what should have been a windfall from the Iran war. Rosneft officials have expressed concern that even a few more months of the war in Ukraine could leave lasting damage across the business, according to people familiar with the matter. The mounting toll to Rosneft and Russia’s wider oil industry helps explain why stopping Ukraine’s strikes on refineries has become such a priority for Moscow. This month, Putin and US President Donald Trump struck a deal opening the door to American purchases of Russian diesel, providing a potential boost as Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks, an important contributor to the squeeze on global diesel supplies. But an attempted energy truce quickly unraveled, narrowing Rosneft’s avenues for relief — and raising the stakes for a government that gets roughly a fifth of federal revenues from oil and gas. This story is based on conversations with people familiar with the situation at Rosneft, expert analysis and a series of documents reviewed by Bloomberg over the last six months, including damage assessments and company plans for protecting and repairing refineries. Vostok Oil was conceived in a different era, when Russia’s oil refineries were not under constant threat of Ukrainian attacks and production was expected only to grow. Laying out his plans to Putin at a Kremlin meeting in February 2020, Sechin described a vast new Arctic oil province that would create jobs and industry in a remote part of the country. One goal, he said, was to turn the Northern Sea Route into a major global energy corridor. The project was also intended to address a longer-term challenge: Many of Russia’s biggest oilfields had been producing since Soviet times, making new reserves increasingly important to offset their decline. The ambition attracted foreign investors, including commodity trading giant Trafigura, which acquired a 10% stake in 2020, and a Vitol-led consortium, which bought another 5% the following year. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 upended those plans. Both Trafigura and the consortium exited, while Western sanctions restricted access to the technology and equipment needed to develop Vostok Oil and build specialized tankers capable of navigating icy waters. As the war dragged on, Ukraine intensified its campaign against Russia’s infrastructure, increasingly targeting the refineries that turn crude oil into fuel. So far this year, Ukrainian drones have carried out at least 114 strikes on Russian refineries, more than double the number over the same period last year, according to a Bloomberg tally, based on public statements from both countries. The attacks have pushed Russian refinery runs to multi-year lows, triggered fuel shortages and forced Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Rosneft has borne a significant share of the damage. The company operates 12 refineries accounting for about a third of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity. Of 15 confirmed drone strikes on the country’s oil-processing plants in September, five targeted major Rosneft facilities supplying fuel to European Russia, the largest consuming region, according to Bloomberg’s tally. Rosneft is “taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants,” and will continue to make sure they are protected, the company said in its statement. “Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices,” it said. In March, while reflecting on Rosneft’s 2025 results, Sechin, a longtime Putin ally, said Russia’s oil producers had faced a “perfect storm” of low oil prices, Western sanctions and soaring borrowing costs. Since then, repeated attacks have forced some of Rosneft’s biggest refineries to operate at reduced capacity or shut altogether. Ryazan has been among the hardest hit, repeatedly coming under attack as Rosneft has sought to restore operations. Another refinery, Syzran, has spent much of the past six months either completely shut or operating at less than a third of capacity, according to data reviewed by Bloomberg, and the company’s Tuapse refinery on the Black Sea coast has been offline since April. Rosneft has managed to restart some refineries within weeks of an attack, only to see them struck again as repairs are completed or nearing completion. The need to repeatedly repair damaged equipment is straining operations and causing costs to pile up to levels that Rosneft officials have privately warned cannot be sustained long-term, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. Some plants have deliberately slowed repairs as a result, stretching work that should take days into weeks, the people said. Efforts to protect the facilities with shipping containers, nets and steel cables have proved ineffective against swarms of drones, according to company plans reviewed by Bloomberg. The damage is particularly difficult to repair when strikes hit complex secondary units such as catalytic crackers, reformers and hydrocrackers, whose parts would previously have been sourced from the West. Sanctions are compounding the problems by restricting access to replacement equipment, forcing Rosneft to rely on Russian-made copies and Chinese imports that can take months to obtain and are not always compatible with existing machinery, people familiar with the matter said. More broadly, the International Energy Agency said drone strikes on Russian refineries are having a “cumulative negative effect.” In September, the agency cut its outlook for Russian oil processing over the next 18 months to around 4 million barrels a day, roughly 30% below prewar levels. The financial toll is mounting. Rosneft’s first-half net income fell by almost a fifth to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion). Its ratio of net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose to 1.8 times at the end of June, the highest in more than five years, according to quarterly statements dating back to 2020, though three reports over the period don’t disclose the ratio, making estimations of the exact size and scope more challenging. To be sure, conditions have improved since then. Middle East disruptions have pushed the price of Russia’s Urals crude used for tax calculations above $90 a barrel, more than double its level at the start of the year, while Moscow is providing billions of rubles in subsidies to domestic fuel producers, including Rosneft, in recent months. Russia’s central bank has also cut its key rate from a record 21% to 14% over the past two years, though Rosneft has complained that the pace of reductions is “clearly insufficient.” The company’s financial picture and the extent of damage to its infrastructure are being closely monitored by the Qatar Investment Authority, which owns 18.46% of Rosneft and has seen its dividend payments fall sharply during the Ukraine war, according to three Qatari officials familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. QIA hopes for a swift end to the conflict so its investment is protected longer-term, one of the people said. QIA declined to comment. Rosneft’s problems have coincided with signs of distress at Credit Bank of Moscow PJSC, which market participants and officials view as being in the orbit of Sechin and his oil giant. MKB, as it is known, is dealing with $8 billion in problem loans, Bloomberg reported last month. That development highlights how both Russia’s energy and banking sectors are coming under strain at the same time, a dynamic that Russian finance officials have expressed concern about, people familiar with the matter said. Rosneft said in its statement that its “relations with MKB, as with other Russian banks, are standard,” adding that “neither Rosneft nor its Chief Executive Officer are or have ever been beneficiaries of MKB.” Rosneft faces another financial challenge: the enormous spending still required at Vostok Oil. The project remains heavily dependent on production from Vankor, a group of established fields that began pumping crude in 2009. Its new Arctic terminal gives Rosneft another route to market for that oil, but does little on its own to increase Russia’s output. Rystad Energy, which has analyzed satellite imagery of construction at the project, expects Vostok Oil to produce about 310,000 barrels a day in 2027, with around 90% coming from the Vankor cluster, where fields have been producing for years. Output could rise to 440,000 barrels a day by 2030 — well short of the roughly 1 million Sechin has promised — with the new Payakha fields contributing only about 80,000 barrels a day, according to the consultancy. Getting the oil to market is another obstacle. Rosneft needs specialized tankers to navigate frigid Arctic waters, but Western sanctions have complicated efforts to build them. At least 30 would be needed by 2030 to transport Vostok Oil’s planned output, according to Sergey Vakulenko, an industry veteran and scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “They simply don’t exist today,” he said. With Russia’s war in Ukraine well into its fifth year, Putin has secured a potential reprieve from Washington. In an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, the Russian president said Russia would partially relax its diesel export ban, releasing thousands of barrels a day into the global market. It’s unclear what, if anything, Russia will receive in return. But in the days since, Ukraine has faced temporary restrictions on its military access to SpaceX satellite technology and US intelligence. For Trump, the immediate concern was closer to home. Diesel prices had surged to near-record levels ahead of November’s congressional elections, squeezed by the war in Iran and disruptions to global fuel supplies. The agreement was intended to help bring prices down, though US officials have acknowledged it is unlikely to have much effect on the international diesel market. Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt refinery strikes that had constrained Russian exports. “Unless President Putin agrees to stop attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure, or President Trump agrees to give Ukraine additional offensive and defensive capabilities, Kyiv is unlikely to abide by a unilateral ceasefire,” said Fernando Ferreira, director of geopolitical risk at Rapidan Energy Group. The limits of the arrangement soon became apparent. Neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed the energy ceasefire Trump subsequently announced, and Kyiv resumed refinery attacks last week after accusing Moscow of continuing strikes on its energy infrastructure. Even if the diplomacy eventually produces a more durable pause, Ukraine is already changing the battlefield. In 2022, its attacks reached targets some 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the border. By July this year, drones had struck the Omsk refinery deep in western Siberia, roughly 2,500 kilometers away. Vostok Oil’s Arctic terminal lies another 800 kilometers beyond that, still outside Ukraine’s demonstrated reach. But the vast distances that have long sheltered Russia’s most remote energy assets offer less reassurance than they once did: If the range of Ukrainian drone strikes continues expanding at its recent pace, Vostok Oil could plausibly come within reach within months. At last month’s opening ceremony, Sechin was still looking ahead. Bundled against the cold beside the Valentin Pikul , he told Putin that Vostok Oil would ship 30 million tons of crude as early as the second half of 2027. It was another sign of how much the project has suffered: The terminal was meant to be ready for that volume two years ago. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Photo courtesy McAllister Towing The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC). The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 vessels. The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook. “The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.” Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. However, their ability to reduce emissions depends heavily on the availability and cost of cleaner fuels. According to WSC, alternative-fuel-capable vessels now account for 65% of containerships and 97% of vehicle carriers on order, measured by deadweight tonnage. That compares with just 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet. Despite that shift, orders for conventionally fueled ships have also increased over the past year as the overall orderbook continues to expand. The mixed picture comes amid continued uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Adoption of the framework was postponed in October 2025, with negotiations set to resume later this year. WSC argues that a global regulatory framework is needed to close the cost gap between conventional fuels and renewable and near-zero-emission alternatives while giving shipowners and fuel producers the certainty needed to invest. Without an international agreement, the industry also faces the prospect of an increasingly fragmented system of regional emissions rules, adding costs and complexity to global shipping. “Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said. The IMO is scheduled to hold its next Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3, with a possible resumed session on the Net-Zero Framework on December 4. “We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework,” Kramek said. “Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email.
