REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Thursday that seven commercial vessels were struck overnight in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including four ships conducting oil transfers, prompting President Donald Trump to accuse Tehran of fabricating attacks to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said four vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were struck simultaneously on Wednesday and caught fire. The vessels were allegedly transferring oil for an American company using routes Iran considers illegal. In a separate claim, the IRGC said three additional vessels struck naval mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires that left them disabled, according to Reuters . None of the seven incidents has been independently confirmed. Iran did not identify the ships, their owners or the American company allegedly involved. There were also no immediate details about casualties or potential oil spills. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which tracks attacks on commercial shipping in the region, has not issued new incident reports corresponding to the claims. President Trump responded Thursday by accusing Iran of inventing attacks as part of an effort to influence oil prices ahead of the November 3 elections. “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict.” The president’s accusation follows weeks of increasingly aggressive Iranian statements claiming that merchant vessels using routes outside Tehran’s control have been struck by mines or other weapons. But the absence of UKMTO reports does not necessarily mean the attacks did not occur. In its October 16 weekly assessment , UKMTO acknowledged that it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were not reporting incidents directly to the organization. UKMTO said it was aware of additional attacks through other sources but could not publish warnings without sufficient verification. That reporting gap has become increasingly important as the United States and Iran offer competing accounts of what is happening in the waterway. The most significant element of Iran’s latest announcement is its claim to have targeted four vessels actively engaged in ship-to-ship oil transfers. If confirmed, the attacks would appear to mark the first reported direct targeting of an active ship-to-ship oil transfer operation during the conflict. Such transfers have become a critical part of the improvised shipping network that has allowed Persian Gulf producers to restore much of their oil exports despite repeated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Under a system operating with U.S. military assistance, tankers make short voyages through the strait, frequently with their AIS transponders switched off, before transferring cargoes to other vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The receiving tankers then carry the oil to international markets. The system has allowed producers to move substantial volumes of crude without relying on routes controlled by Iran, although at extraordinary cost. The International Energy Agency reported Wednesday that tanker freight costs from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed above $37 per barrel, more than five times prewar levels. For a fully loaded 2-million-barrel VLCC, that translates to more than $74 million in freight costs alone. The location of Iran’s latest alleged attacks, in the northern Persian Gulf, is distinct from the Gulf of Oman transfer operations used by the U.S.-facilitated shuttle system. There is currently no independent evidence connecting the four vessels to that network. Nevertheless, a confirmed attack on vessels during cargo transfers would represent a potentially significant expansion of the threat to regional oil shipping. Iran’s latest claims also follow a series of announcements alleging that tankers have struck naval mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorization. Those claims have repeatedly been challenged by maritime security authorities. In its October 18 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) addressed Iranian statements that two supertankers had struck mines the previous day, saying there was “no substantiation to these claims.” U.S. Central Command has also rejected previous Iranian mine-strike announcements as false, accusing the IRGC of attempting to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation. However, JMIC continues to warn of a credible threat of renewed mining in and around the strait’s traffic separation scheme. Its latest assessment maintains the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, with further deliberate attacks considered highly likely. Trump’s assertion that more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the conflict also comes amid conflicting assessments of the recovery in Gulf exports. Overall Middle East oil shipments have approached or exceeded prewar levels in recent weeks, aided by an expanded network of pipelines, short-haul tanker voyages and offshore transfers. But the recovery in total exports does not necessarily mean that more oil is moving through the strait itself. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal cited by gCaptain , flows through Hormuz, including offshore transfers, remained at approximately 82% of prewar levels, even as overall regional exports recovered. UKMTO’s latest weekly overview also recorded just 254 vessel transits during the seven days ending October 14, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Those figures include U.S.-reported facilitated transits that UKMTO says it cannot independently verify. The figures measure different things—vessel movements, oil flows through Hormuz and overall regional exports—but illustrate the difficulty of determining how much shipping has actually recovered. Meanwhile, the security situation continues to deteriorate. UKMTO documented 12 attacks during the reporting period ending October 16, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz. One vessel was lost, two were disabled or left not under command, and the outcomes of three others remained uncertain. The escalation has included the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride following an October 13 attack, as well as strikes on tankers operating inside the Persian Gulf. Iran’s latest announcement adds another seven potential incidents to an already incomplete picture. For now, neither Tehran’s claim that seven vessels were attacked nor Trump’s assertion that the incidents were fabricated has been independently established. What is clear is that merchant ships continue to face serious threats, even as oil producers find increasingly costly ways to keep cargoes moving. Windward intelligence report highlights tanker and tug attacks, threats to subsea cables, an emerging oil spill and a sanctioned Russian tanker testing U.S. naval restrictions. Maritime security risks across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman are expanding beyond attacks on commercial tankers, with threats now extending to subsea communications infrastructure, offshore support vessels and coastal facilities. An October 22 intelligence report from Windward Maritime identifies five developments that illustrate the widening scope of the conflict and its implications for commercial shipping, energy transportation and regional infrastructure. Iran Threatens Subsea Communications Cables Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has identified subsea internet cables crossing the Strait of Hormuz as potential targets. On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi warned that new targets and weapons would be unveiled, citing seven major communications cables beneath the strait. Windward identifies six operational cable systems crossing Hormuz, with additional systems scheduled for 2027. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are particularly vulnerable because their subsea communications routes to markets outside the Gulf pass through the strait. For Iraq, the vulnerability is compounded by all three operational cables landing at Al Faw. Disruptions could affect regional communications infrastructure well beyond commercial shipping. However, Windward notes that two cable systems also connect to Iran, meaning attacks could damage Iranian connectivity. Live subsea cable landings per country across the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, with countries ranked by exposure. Source: Windward Maritime AITM Platform. Small-Boat Attack Signals Changing Tactics On October 16, a Liberia-flagged Suezmax tanker was likely struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat approximately 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia. According to a UK Maritime Trade Operations advisory cited by Windward, the attack damaged the tanker's aft port quarter, although no casualties were reported. The vessel continued sailing, reportedly carrying approximately 1.09 million barrels of Saudi and UAE crude bound for Kuwait. Earlier that day, another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile nearby, prompting the safe evacuation of its crew. Windward considers the suspected small-boat attack significant because previous incidents predominantly involved drones or projectiles concentrated around Hormuz. The development suggests threats to shipping are extending deeper into the Gulf, potentially affecting war-risk assessments for regional port calls. Tug Attack Threatens Gulf Oil Transfer Operations A Netherlands-flagged tug, identified by TradeWinds as JIF Barracuda, was reportedly struck by two unidentified projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE, on October 18. One crew member suffered minor injuries, but the tug continued its voyage. UKMTO did not attribute responsibility for the attack. Windward identifies the incident as the second tug strike since the conflict began and the 27th maritime attack recorded during October. The location is significant. Khor Fakkan, Fujairah and Sohar support extensive ship-to-ship crude oil transfers outside Hormuz. Windward estimates that these anchorages handled approximately 3.97 million barrels per day in transfers during October 12–14, representing roughly half the crude shipped from the Gulf of Oman during that period. Attacks on tugs threaten the support infrastructure needed to maintain tanker movements, cargo transfers and salvage operations. Tanker Oil Leak Threatens UAE Coastline Satellite imagery collected October 19 identified a VLCC-size tanker apparently leaking oil approximately 25 kilometers north of Umm Al Quwain. Windward observed a slick extending approximately 1.5 km behind the vessel. Its drift modeling projected possible shoreline contamination beginning October 22, with oil potentially approaching Hamriyah Port, Ajman Port, coastal mangroves and desalination infrastructure through October 24. The company cautions that its projections do not account for cleanup operations or the leak being stopped. Sanctioned Russian Tanker Tests U.S. Naval Line A Russian-flagged oil and chemical tanker approached and crossed a U.S. Navy restriction line inbound to the Gulf of Oman on October 18. According to Windward, the vessel slowed from nine knots to approximately one knot, loitered and subsequently reversed course toward the Arabian Sea on October 19. The EU- and UK-sanctioned tanker was assessed as potentially carrying approximately 65,400 barrels of naphtha. Windward describes the movement as an apparent test of the naval restriction line, although the vessel's intended destination remains unknown. Taken together, the five developments point to an increasingly complex operating environment for shipowners, charterers and marine service providers. Beyond the direct threat to vessels, the conflict is exposing vulnerabilities in the infrastructure that supports regional trade, energy exports and maritime operations.

The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has named the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) and Ørsted the winners of the 2026 NOIA Environmental, Social, & Governance (ESG) Excellence Awards. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran. The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054. Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee. The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia. While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict. QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio. “This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy. For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations. The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion. The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. articles.title: Saipem and Egypt’s MDC seal pact to target MENA offshore drilling market
articles.summary: Saipem and Modern Drilling Company (MDC) are joining forces to pursue strategic offshore drilling opportunities across Egypt and the MENA region.
articles.body: Collaboration October 22, 2026 · 20 hours ago Saipem and Egypt’s MDC seal pact to target MENA offshore drilling market Saipem and Modern Drilling Company (MDC) are joining forces to pursue strategic offshore drilling opportunities across Egypt and the MENA region. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Saipem Italy’s engineering, drilling, and construction services giant Saipem is expanding its footprint in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region by teaming up with Egypt’s Modern Drilling Company, a drilling contractor, through a new non-exclusive partnership agreement aimed at capturing upcoming offshore drilling opportunities in the region. Saipem and Modern Drilling Company have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore new cooperation opportunities in offshore drilling, starting from the Egyptian market and potentially extending to other countries of mutual interest. The Italian giant highlights that this agreement lays the foundation for a non-exclusive strategic cooperation aimed at identifying and developing new business initiatives in offshore drilling services. The two companies will determine the most effective collaboration model for each opportunity, including the assessment of joint ventures, consortia, or dedicated agreements for individual projects. The development of the partnership will be overseen by a joint coordination committee responsible for monitoring market developments, identifying projects of mutual interest, and defining the next steps of the cooperation. In addition, the scope of the agreement may include the sharing of expertise and experience, support in project execution, asset management activities, and training services. Saipem emphasizes that this MoU strengthens its position in a strategic market such as Egypt and aims to leverage new industrial synergies to capture growth opportunities in the offshore energy sector. The European player recently secured multiple deals, including the commissioning services contract for a floating production unit (FPU) destined for Türkiye’s largest natural gas field. articles.title: FEED job for Barents Sea FPSO topsides goes to Aibel
articles.summary: Equinor has booked Aibel for its oil project's topsides engineering study as partners eye a concept selection by late 2026.
articles.body: Project & Tenders October 22, 2026 · 20 hours ago FEED job for Barents Sea FPSO topsides goes to Aibel Equinor has booked Aibel for its oil project's topsides engineering study as partners eye a concept selection by late 2026. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Wisting FPSO illustration Courtesy of Aibel Equinor, Norway’s state-owned energy giant, has entrusted Aibel, a compatriot energy services company, with a front-end engineering and design (FEED) study for the topsides of a production vessel destined for an oil project in the Barents Sea. The contract award for front-end engineering and design of the Wisting production vessel’s topsides was handed out to Aibel following a competitive tender involving Norwegian suppliers. This deal covers front-end engineering and further maturation of the design to provide a basis for a decision on project execution, with an option for engineering, procurement, and project management (EPma). The partnership, encompassing Equinor (42.5%, operator), Aker BP (27.5%), Petoro (20%), and INPEX Idemitsu Norge (10%), plans to do a concept selection and decide whether to progress Wisting towards the end of 2026, with the final investment decision (FID) planned for late 2027. Mads Andersen , Aibel’s President and CEO, commented: "This is a very important contract for us, particularly in terms of maintaining our centres of expertise following a period in which we have recently completed major deliveries both to the Norwegian Continental Shelf and to European offshore wind projects. “The Wisting development has the potential to become a major new-build project that will be of great importance to Norwegian supplier industry.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Investment decision for Barents Sea project postponed amid cost growth in supply industry 3 min read According to Aibel, the FEED contract for the topside modules for the production vessel at the Wisting field will provide work for approximately 250 employees at Aibel’s offices in Asker, supported by personnel in Haugesund. The work will begin immediately and is expected to be completed in late 2027. Equinor claims that the contract for fabrication of the topside modules will be awarded at a later stage. Wisting location; Source: Equinor Trond Bokn , Equinor's Senior Vice President for Project Development, said: “We are at an early stage in the development of Wisting, and considerable work remains to develop a project that is profitable and feasible. “If we succeed, it will contribute to energy security for Europe and generate revenues for Norwegian society. Wisting will generate activity in the Norwegian supplier industry and in local communities in the north over a 30-year period.” The development of Wisting would offer significant opportunities for the Norwegian supplier industry in engineering and equipment deliveries, as drilling, wells, and subsea development account for half of the total investment. Related Articles Fossil Energy Subsea7 and OneSubsea hired to work on Wisting and Bay du Nord oil projects 3 min read Operations at the project are expected to last for 30 years, generating activity for the Norwegian supplier industry, helping to sustain industrial jobs and supporting activity in local communities in the north. “We are pleased to welcome Aibel to the Wisting team. This FEED contract will form part of the overall basis for a potential investment decision. We will work with the suppliers on improvements to enable the project to be realised,” added Bokn. articles.title: Miros Launches 3D Vessel View For Sea-State Monitoring
articles.summary: Miros, a Norwegian specialist in radar-based real-time ocean surface measurement, has introduced a 3D vessel view providing crews and operators with a consolidated view of the accurately measured sea state surrounding their vessel. The new 3D interface in WaveSystem…
articles.body: Miros Launches 3D Vessel View For Sea-State Monitoring Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Miros Miros, a Norwegian specialist in radar-based real-time ocean surface measurement, has introduced a 3D vessel view providing crews and operators with a consolidated view of the accurately measured sea state surrounding their vessel. The new 3D interface in WaveSystem, a wave monitoring system for weather-critical offshore vessel operations, shows where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. The feature is included for WaveSystem subscribers worldwide at no additional cost. Wave conditions can differ around a vessel due to wave direction, vessel heading, hull geometry, shielding, and measurement location. Where multiple measurement sources are installed, comparing readings can help teams clearly understand differences between measurement areas and sea conditions affecting specific working areas. Bridge and deck crew can easily assess conditions port and starboard, check the waves at a specific working area such as a gangway or ROV launch point, and spot differences between measurement areas before they affect the operation, turning a weather-critical operation into a controlled one. The visualization shows measurement sources, areas, and values in relation to the vessel. It does not represent a reconstructed 3D sea surface.

articles.title: Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey
articles.summary: TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies.
articles.body: Vessels October 22, 2026 · 21 hours ago Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email N5K on back of RV Poseidon with the rig working close to it in the background Credit: Ivan Svrcek/TDI-Brooks U.S.-headquartered geotechnical and offshore survey research and service company TDI-Brooks has wrapped up a critical geotechnical campaign for Cook Inlet LNG, a strategic initiative designed to secure natural gas supplies for Southcentral Alaska, delivering vital subsurface data to support the project's anchor selection and helping bring the developer’s floating import terminal aspirations closer to reality. TDI-Brooks has concluded a geotechnical project for the Cook Inlet LNG project (CI LNG) in Cook Inlet, Alaska, providing its Neptune N5K cone penetration testing (CPT) system for an anchor site characterization study. The work supported the project developer by collecting subsurface soil data to inform anchor selection. According to the U.S. player, the study covered different locations within the project site with a scope of 16 CPTs in water depths ranging from 10 to 25 meters. Operations were conducted from the R/V Poseidon , a third-party vessel working in the region, demonstrating the firm’s ability to deploy specialized geotechnical equipment aboard locally available vessels. The Neptune N5K is part of the company’s range of portable toolkits available for deployment worldwide, which allow clients to pair regional vessel resources with TDI-Brooks’ equipment and technical expertise, providing flexible support for offshore site investigations and infrastructure projects. The Cook Inlet LNG project is an energy security initiative designed to address declining natural gas reserves in the Cook Inlet basin of Southcentral Alaska to stave off a potential energy shortfall for heating and electricity by serving as a near-term bridge solution to import gas. The project is designed to use a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) anchored offshore east of West Foreland, near the existing Osprey production platform, utilizing existing subsea pipelines to minimize environmental and construction footprints. TDI-Brooks’ geotechnical study was done to test the seafloor soil properties to figure out how to safely anchor the FSRU and its infrastructure in Cook Inlet's harsh marine environment. The completion of this study comes months after the U.S. firm was hired by Delfin LNG to provide offshore geophysical and geotechnical survey services for the Delfin deepwater port project offshore Louisiana. articles.title: Nexans, Red Eléctrica to tie Mallorca and Menorca closer with new Balearic power link
articles.summary: Nexans and Red Eléctrica are future-proofing the Balearic Islands' power grid with a strategic new Mallorca-Menorca interconnection.
articles.body: Project & Tenders October 22, 2026 · 22 hours ago Nexans, Red Eléctrica to tie Mallorca and Menorca closer with new Balearic power link Nexans and Red Eléctrica are future-proofing the Balearic Islands' power grid with a strategic new Mallorca-Menorca interconnection. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Nexans French cable systems designer and manufacturer Nexans has been tapped as the preferred supplier for a 132 kV power cable link designed to strengthen the security and resilience of the Balearic Islands’ electricity network and slash Menorca's reliance on fossil fuels. Nexans has been selected as the preferred supplier by Red Eléctrica , Redeia 's subsidiary responsible for electricity transmission and the operation of Spain's power systems, for the Mallorca-Menorca 3 interconnection project, a strategic power infrastructure initiative designed to fortify the security and resilience of electricity supply in the Balearic Islands. The tender launched by Red Eléctrica for this project specifies that the execution of the agreement will initiate a six-month engineering phase for a new 132 kV high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) cable link between Mallorca and Menorca and lay the foundation for a future engineering, procurement, construction, and installation (EPCI) contract. According to the French giant, this project represents the next stage in the development of the electrical connection between the two islands and will support the long-term reliability and stability of the regional power system, enabling Menorca Island to significantly reduce its dependency on fossil fuel electricity generation upon delivery. Nexans will conduct engineering activities for a comprehensive cable system incorporating both subsea and land cable infrastructure, building on its longstanding experience delivering complex interconnection projects and its established presence in the region. The project will leverage the company’s expertise across engineering, manufacturing, and installation, with particular attention to be given to environmental stewardship throughout project planning and execution, reflecting the ecological sensitivity of the project area. The new interconnection also builds on the European firm's previous contribution to the existing electrical link between Mallorca and Menorca and further strengthens the long-standing collaboration between the two companies. Pascal Radue , EVP of PWR-Transmission at Nexans, commented: "Nexans is proud to have been selected by Red Eléctrica for this strategic project. The Mallorca-Menorca interconnection is an important infrastructure investment that will help reinforce network resilience and support the energy transition in the Balearic Islands. “This agreement reflects the confidence placed in Nexans' end-to-end capabilities and our track record in delivering reliable and sustainable electrification solutions." The preferred supplier role for this western Mediterranean project comes shortly after Nexans kicked off the production of 525 kV high-voltage direct current (HVDC) subsea cables for the LanWin2 offshore grid connection. articles.title: EnerMech takes on ‘major’ UK CCS gig but keeps project details under wraps
articles.summary: EnerMech has revealed a new carbon capture and storage (CCS) job in the UK, though project details and the operator remain undisclosed.
articles.body: Carbon Capture Usage & Storage October 22, 2026 · 23 hours ago EnerMech takes on ‘major’ UK CCS gig but keeps project details under wraps EnerMech has revealed a new carbon capture and storage (CCS) job in the UK, though project details and the operator remain undisclosed. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email EnerMech's new pre-commissioning and commissioning contract is for a UK carbon capture development. Source: EnerMech While pertinent information about the operator and project itself is being kept behind closed doors, Aberdeen-headquartered integrated solutions specialist EnerMech has unveiled a fresh assignment to support a carbon capture and storage development in the United Kingdom (UK), which will form a cornerstone of the nation’s decarbonization roadmap. EnerMech has been awarded a contract to provide specialist pre-commissioning and commissioning services for a carbon capture and storage project it describes as a “major” development in the UK, which strengthens the firm’s role in supporting complex energy and lower-carbon infrastructure developments around the world. Charles ‘Chuck’ Davison, Jr. , EnerMech’s CEO, commented: “This development represents an important investment in the infrastructure required to support large-scale carbon capture and storage. Our selection reflects the strength of our specialist pre-commissioning and commissioning capabilities, the experience of our people and our ability to execute complex scopes safely and efficiently. “As investment in decarbonization and energy infrastructure continues to grow, EnerMech is proud to bring its technical expertise to projects that will help advance the next generation of UK and international CCS developments.” The Aberdeen-based firm will deliver a range of specialist services to support the safe, efficient and compliant readiness of critical transportation and storage infrastructure, including nitrogen services, dewatering, drying, pigging and leak testing, supported by integrated onshore and offshore execution. This development will form part of the infrastructure needed to transport and permanently store captured carbon dioxide emissions, supporting the nation’s wider decarbonization ambitions. The scope draws on EnerMech’s experience delivering comparable, technically demanding pipeline, subsea and commissioning programs internationally, including long-distance dewatering and drying, engineered pigging, high-volume nitrogen operations and tightly coordinated onshore-offshore campaigns. Nuno de Sousa , SVP Energy Solutions & Western Hemisphere at EnerMech, said: “Carbon transportation and storage infrastructure presents distinct technical and operational challenges, particularly when preparing critical subsea systems for safe and reliable operation. “Our multi-disciplined teams combine engineering expertise, specialist equipment and disciplined execution with extensive experience gained across major pipeline, subsea and commissioning scopes around the world.” This CCS assignment in the UK comes shortly after EnerMech won a five-year extension of its deal with Chevron in Australia.
